memory_update.text: DPZ is the cleanest reference model for the node because its royalty stream is reinforced by vertically integrated supply chain, procurement scale, advertising fund participation, and first-party digital demand capture.
YUM should remain a reference anchor for multi-brand franchise supply-chain consolidation and global supplier leverage, but it is too widely followed to be the main alpha-discovery target.

WEST is a plausible underfollowed B2B restaurant/foodservice beverage supplier in the preferred small-cap range; survival in later layers depends on verifying foodservice customer mix, contracts, plant utilization, margins, and leverage.

FARM is a micro-cap speculative shadow candidate with potentially direct foodservice exposure, but it is below the preferred market-cap threshold and needs stringent liquidity, customer-retention, and restructuring diligence.

Need a later pass on non-brand suppliers to franchisee capex and remodel cycles: POS/loyalty software, kitchen equipment, refrigeration, maintenance, uniforms, packaging, sanitation, distribution, and approved food suppliers.

FARM should be tracked as a speculative_shadow candidate for restaurant/franchise beverage inputs, DSD route economics, coffee-machine service, and obscure private-label customer exposure; survival requires current filing evidence of foodservice/franchise customer relevance and balance-sheet viability.

WEST should be tracked as an underfollowed B2B coffee/tea/extract supplier potentially tied to foodservice operators and private-label restaurant beverage programs; key proof points are named customers, contract durability, capacity utilization, margin improvement, and leverage control.
THS is a possible hidden supplier through private-label food and beverage manufacturing and the Farmer Brothers asset transaction, but direct restaurant-franchise exposure remains a coverage gap.

Domino's and Yum support the broader node thesis that franchise systems are increasingly using centralized procurement, unified supplier management, and supply-chain scale to protect franchisee unit economics under inflation pressure.

Need a later targeted search for public restaurant equipment and service vendors tied to franchisee capex, remodels, kitchen automation, beverage systems, refrigeration, HVAC, maintenance, sanitation, and approved-vendor status; this pass only had strong supplied evidence for beverage/coffee and franchisor supply-chain examples.

PAR is a stronger underfollowed restaurant-tech candidate for the franchise unit-economics node because it sells POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and back-office systems directly into enterprise restaurants and franchisees.

WEST is a plausible small-cap second-order beverage supplier for restaurant systems, but customer specificity, foodservice revenue mix, debt, and commodity exposure must be verified before promotion beyond Layer 1.
FARM is a speculative micro-cap exception with direct foodservice and restaurant-supplier relevance; liquidity, customer concentration, and post-asset-sale business mix are key survival tests.
OLO would have been a clean digital-ordering underfollowed candidate, but it is no longer a US-listed public equity after the 2025 Thoma Bravo acquisition and NYSE delisting.
DPZ should remain a reference leader for this node because its franchise royalty model is reinforced by owned supply-chain infrastructure and direct digital demand capture.
MIDD is a plausible underfollowed second-order beneficiary of restaurant franchise remodels, new-unit capex, kitchen automation, throughput improvement, and energy/labor efficiency needs.
PAR is a plausible small-cap restaurant software candidate tied to POS, loyalty, payments, and first-party data capture, but needs verification of enterprise franchise wins and ARR quality.

FARM is a speculative micro-cap shadow candidate because it may be a hidden coffee/beverage supplier to restaurant systems, but its post-divestiture exposure and balance-sheet risk must be checked before promotion.

Next Layer 1C should search approved-vendor relationships across QSR equipment, beverage, packaging, maintenance, and procurement platforms because many beneficiaries may be classified outside restaurants.

node: Franchise royalty systems and unit-economics flywheel
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: This pass expands the direct public-company universe around franchise royalty systems and franchisee unit-economics support. The reference lane is anchored by large franchisors with scale advantages in royalties, advertising, procurement, digital demand capture, and franchisee standards. The underfollowed lane focuses on B2B suppliers whose demand may compound with restaurant unit growth, remodels, beverage programs, approved-vendor relationships, and foodservice procurement complexity. No recommendation is made; these are research candidates for evidence tracking. This Layer 1B pass expands the universe around scarce or underfollowed suppliers that can influence restaurant franchisee unit economics through procurement scale, approved-vendor access, beverage/coffee inputs, foodservice distribution, kitchen/service equipment, and supply-chain infrastructure. Reference leaders such as Domino's and Yum are useful context because they show why franchisors care about centralized procurement and system-level cost control, but the discovery lane is more interesting in small/mid-cap B2B suppliers such as Farmer Brothers and Westrock Coffee, plus foodservice supplier platforms whose economics may depend on franchisee capex, remodel cycles, and approved-product status. Expanded one node around franchise royalty systems and franchisee unit economics.
